title: Prayer, fasting, almsgiving (Matthew 6:1–18)
hookLine: Lent's three practices, done in secret

cards: You've seen it online. Someone posts a photo from the soup kitchen, well lit, with a caption about giving back. Someone else announces they're on day three of a fast.
Someone's been up since five for prayer. None of it is bad. But something about it is odd, and Jesus named it long before phones.
On Ash Wednesday, the Gospel at Catholic Mass is his answer: three practices, and one condition. Today: almsgiving, and its two companions.

teach.b: In the Sermon on the Mount, in Matthew chapter six, Jesus takes the three great religious practices of his own Jewish tradition, giving to the poor, prayer and fasting, and says the same thing about each: don't do it to be seen.
On giving, in the Douay-Rheims: "But when thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth."
On prayer: "But thou when thou shalt pray, enter into thy chamber, and having shut the door, pray to thy Father in secret." On fasting: wash your face and look normal, so no one can tell.
Each time the promise is the same: your Father who sees in secret will repay you. These three became the backbone of Lent. Prayer turns you toward God.
Fasting turns you away from your own appetites. Almsgiving turns you toward your neighbor.
Alms comes, through Latin, from the Greek eleemosyne, mercy. Giving alms is doing mercy, and Catholics count more than money here: time, attention, a meal, a visit, patience.
Some parishes hand out a small cardboard box at the start of Lent, and families drop in what they save by eating simply, to be given away at Easter.

teach.h: THY FATHER WHO SEETH IN SECRET.
teach.b: Why secret? The moment you do good in order to be seen, the audience becomes the point. Jesus calls that having your reward already.

Done in secret, the good deed stays pointed at God and at the person you're helping. And there's a freedom in it: nobody's watching, so you don't have to perform. Tomorrow, a walk around the church walls.

how: In Lent Catholics take up prayer, fasting and almsgiving, often giving up something, adding a practice, and putting what they save into a parish collection box for the poor, given at Easter.

o: giving up food for a set season
paying a set tax to your parish
giving to people in need, as mercy

games.q: what's inside the three — tap the pairs.

s: alms comes from a Greek word for mercy
eleemosyne, through Latin; giving alms is doing mercy.
Catholics count time, attention, meals, visits and patience too.
Jesus tells people to fast publicly as a witness
he says wash your face and look normal, so no one can tell.

games.q: you've just given a large gift to someone in need. a friend asks what you've been up to. what does Matthew 6 suggest?
o: post about it so others give too.
keep it quiet: let not thy left hand know.
games.why: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth." the good done in secret stays pointed at God and the person helped.

practice: Pick one of the three: a few quiet minutes of prayer, door shut; a small fast, skipping a snack, a scroll or a second coffee; or one act of mercy nobody will know about, money, time or a kind word.
Picture yourself doing it, and decide you won't mention it to anyone. If you pray, you can offer it to God.

wordCard.voice: Almsgiving. From the Greek for mercy. Giving to those in need, one of Lent's three practices, done so the left hand doesn't know. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: mercy, and so alms. The English word alms is a worn-down form of it.

carryVoice: Your line: in secret. Prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and no audience. That's day one hundred forty-nine.
